hints: Focus on what is made inside the RBC from carbon dioxide and then needs to leave in large amounts to be carried in the plasma.
Remember the rule of electrical neutrality: if lots of negative hydrogencarbonate ions leave the RBC, another negative ion must enter to keep the charge balanced.
walkthrough:
**Recall how CO2 is carried**

Think of respiring tissues releasing CO2. Most of it diffuses from plasma into the RBC. This is the starting point, not the chloride shift itself.

Key reaction inside RBC (catalysed by carbonic anhydrase):
$$CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3 \rightarrow H^+ + HCO_3^-$$

**See the charge problem**

The $H^+$ is mopped up by haemoglobin to form haemoglobinic acid. That leaves lots of $HCO_3^-$ (hydrogencarbonate ions) building up inside the RBC. If they just diffused out into the plasma, the RBC would be left positively charged and the plasma negatively charged.

**Apply the chloride shift**

To keep electrical neutrality, for every $HCO_3^-$ that diffuses out of the RBC into the plasma, one $Cl^-$ (chloride ion) diffuses from the plasma into the RBC. That one-for-one swap of negative ions is the chloride shift. This lets plasma carry most $HCO_3^-$ to the lungs.

options.A: CO2 does enter the RBC, but chloride ions move into the RBC, not out of it, so the directions are wrong.
options.B: Correct. Hydrogencarbonate leaves the RBC for the plasma and chloride enters the RBC, keeping positive and negative ions balanced.
options.C: This confuses the chloride shift with the Bohr shift. It is H+ ions (not chloride) that promote oxygen release from haemoglobin.
options.D: This reverses the true movement. In respiring tissues, hydrogencarbonate moves out of the RBC and chloride moves in, not the other way round.
